title_original: Global AI certification standard in development by Qatar’s Film Committee, John Penotti
excerpt_original: “We want to make sure there is a global standard,” says Penotti.

blocks.text: Crazy Rich Asians producer John Penotti is developing an AI certification standard with the Film Committee at Media City Qatar.
Penotti discussed the work-in-progress standard during a panel at Doha Film Festival’s Doha Industry Days.

“A lot of our work for the last year has been creating an AI certification opportunity, so that there’s a standard,” said Penotti, on a discussion titled ‘Swipe, Watch, Repeat: The Rise of Microdramas’. “We want to make sure there is some global standard, to make sure this is an asset that could both generate revenue to start, and benefit the author throughout its life cycle.

“Starting here at the Film Committee over the last year or so, we’ve been developing a process by which an AI certification is globally recognised. We’re doing it with the Film Committee’s help and support, and ability to broaden our global partners, so it has an access point everywhere around the world.”

Penotti was speaking on the panel with Anatolii Kasianov, co-founder and co-CEO of AI entertainment company Holywater Tech, which builds vertical storytelling platforms and content for them, and AI-assisted content tools.

The producer said a group of partners has convened on the standard, with further details to be announced in the coming fortnight. The standard will exist “so that the author knows ‘I don’t just have an idea. I need to build a sustainable career with this, so it’s not fleeting’” said the producer. “The idea is to expand on the extraordinary work Anatolii is doing, so that both for your model, for your financing, and then for the creator’s financing, those interests are melded together.

“Then you could go to a distributor, where the distributors [know] this is reliable, I have the rights to do this. There’s an ethical authorship that we could prove, that has a stamp, that says ‘This is what the author intended, and we’re going to protect that throughout its lifespan.”

Returning to the standard later in the discussion, Penotti made an analogy to the change from the early days of Hollywood, when studios had writers, actors and directors under exclusive deals. “It’s moving from that Hollywood system to ‘where’s the value created?’ It’s with the person who came up with the idea. But they can’t do it without pouring cash and distribution into it..

“What we’re hoping to do is not rules, but some structural organisation that gives a long-term impact. Hollywood has changed; there are no longer those stables of writers shoved in some bungalow in Burbank. Now, you have an ability to reach around the world, but still provide the same kind of underlying infrastructure that allows consistent financing to find these productions.”

Kasianov offered a blunt prediction for the production workforce. “In a couple of years, physical production will not be that relevant anymore, since anybody in the room [will be able to] create high-quality films. It will all come down to ideas,” said the Ukrainian executive.

“Even in our case, with so many AI automation workflows, we still need to have human showrunners who create stories. I think that will never change. AI just helps you to do it 100 times faster to get to the finish point.”

In response to an audience question about how much micro-drama content in the US is filmed under union protections, Kasianov said “The majority of content is filmed with non-unions because of how fast and cost-efficient it is. But the salaries we’re paying to stars, to lead actors, they’re almost on a par or in some cases higher than what unions require. The main challenge is time. When you shoot something in six-to-seven days, very efficiently around 10 pages per day, you can [do it much more cheaply].”

“That is a huge issue,” said Penotti. “I’m a guild member; I’m sensitive to my brethren who make their living by monetising their ideas. There’s a huge race happening; certain guilds have been able to quickly digest this. It’s just at the beginning.

“As it becomes clear the amount of revenue Anatolii and other companies like his are generating, the natural step will be to make sure that those guild restrictions don’t limit the ability to create, but they support it. There’s a lot of hard work [to do], basic agreements are going to be adjusted, because it’s so new. Our certification is going to help with that because we’re going to give a standard by which you could start building rules around it.”
The Doha Industry Days conclude tomorrow (Saturday, November 21) with the festival running until Friday 27.
